newsitem.title: USA: Prosecution rests in McVeigh trial penalty phase.
newsitem.headline: Prosecution rests in McVeigh trial penalty phase.

text.p: Jurors deciding the fate of convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh on Friday heard the end of the prosecution's case, many crying at the words of a little boy who still makes Valentines for his dead mother.

The prosecution rested its case after presenting 38 witnesses in the penalty phase of McVeigh's trial. The jury must decide if he will be executed or spend life in prison for the April 19, 1995 bombing that left 168 people dead.

McVeigh's attorneys were to begin presenting their opening statement and witnesses on Friday afternoon in an effort to keep their client off death row. He was convicted on Monday of murder and conspiracy in the bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal office building.

A letter written by 9-year-old Clint Seidl and read aloud by his father capped off the prosecution's case after a trail of witnesses who have testified since Wednesday about the impact of the bombing on their lives and their loved ones.
The youngster was to have been the only child to testify in the trial but U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch decided this week that his testimony would be too inflammatory.
Despite the death of his mother in the bombing, he wrote in the letter, "I still make my mom Mother's Day and Valentine cards like the other kids."
As he has throughout his trial, McVeigh betrayed no emotion but he appeared to be listening and watching intently.

With several jurors dabbing away tears, the prosecution also showed a videotape of Nekia McCloud, who was 4 when the bomb left her severely and permanently brain-damaged. The girl showed few physical scars but was clearly disoriented, easily distracted and unable to respond to even basic questions. She was seen smashing a doll in frustration over her helplessness.

Oklahoma City Police Officer Don Browning spoke of his frustration and guilt after spending six weeks looking for victims in the bombed-out building. The ex-Marine and Vietnam veteran said the experience left him plagued by a recurring nightmare in which he is still crawling through the rubble.
"I begin to feel the ground tremble beneath me. It turns into a growl, a monstrous growl. I turn and run. The kids are crying. I feel so very guilty I didn't get to them," he said.

Defence attorneys were expected to introduce testimony from members of McVeigh's family in their effort to present mitigating factors and convince the jury not to sentence him to death. They also were expected to present witnesses who knew McVeigh during his stint as an Army sergeant during the Gulf War.
But after the painful and sometimes gruesome testimony from prosecution witnesses, the defence's task could be very difficult, said Denver attorney Scott Robinson, who has followed the case closely.

"It would be impossible to hear the stories of these people and not be touched over and over again," Robinson said. "No juror can vote for life in the face of such poignant testimony from victims. Timothy McVeigh has no chance of escaping a sentence of death from this jury."
